title: Phase Portrait
body:
A picture of a system's trajectories in state space instead of a formula for them. For
$\mathbf{x}' = A\mathbf{x}$, plot $x_2$ against $x_1$ with time as a parameter along each curve.
The right hand side is a [[Vector Field]], and the trajectories are the curves tangent to it
everywhere.

The reason to draw one: **you can read stability off it without solving anything**. For nonlinear
systems, which is most of them, that is often all you can get.

## What to find

1. **Equilibria**: points where $\mathbf{x}' = \mathbf{0}$, so the system stays put. For a linear
   system the origin, and only the origin, unless $A$ is singular
2. **Eigenvalues of $A$**: they classify the equilibrium, per the table in
   [[Systems of Differential Equations]]
3. **Eigenvectors**: real ones are **straight-line trajectories**, since a solution starting on an
   eigenvector direction stays on it and only scales. They are the skeleton the other curves bend
   around
4. **Direction of travel**: arrows point away from a positive eigenvalue's direction and toward a
   negative one's

## Stability, in one line

$$
\text{stable} \iff \text{every eigenvalue has negative real part}
$$

Real part negative gives decay, positive gives growth, zero is the borderline case where the linear
picture stops being trustworthy. For a nonlinear system, linearise at each equilibrium by taking the
Jacobian (the [[Matrix]] of [[Partial Derivative|partials]] of the right hand side) and apply the
same table locally. The Jacobian at an equilibrium is the closest linear system to the real one,
which is [[Linear Approximation]] applied to a vector field.

**A saddle is the case worth recognising**: attracting along one eigenvector, repelling along the
other, so almost every nearby trajectory eventually leaves. The same geometry as a saddle point in
[[Multivariable Optimization]], and it is not a coincidence: gradient descent on a surface is the
system $\mathbf{x}' = -\nabla f$, so the critical points of $f$ are its equilibria and their
Hessian is its Jacobian.
